meta.title: Zscaler — Jay Chaudhry's cloud-native zero-trust SASE platform from the 2007 founding through the AI security pivot
meta.abstract: Zscaler, Inc. (NASDAQ: ZS) is the principal US-domiciled cloud-native zero-trust security platform — its Zero Trust Exchange replaces legacy network security stacks (firewalls, VPNs, proxies) with a cloud-delivered Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) and Security Service Edge (SSE) architecture. Founded in 2007 by Jay Chaudhry, who remains chairman and CEO. Headquartered in San Jose, California. Strategic narrative through 2024-2026 centered on platform expansion beyond core Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) and Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) into AI-driven security operations, data protection, and IoT/OT security — plus the broader SASE consolidation against Palo Alto Networks (Prisma), Netskope, Cisco, and emerging Cloudflare zero-trust offerings.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Zscaler's defining strategic move through 2024 and into the frozen May 2026 window was not merely defending the zero-trust ground it had already won. It was broadening the economic perimeter of the Zero Trust Exchange itself. Having established Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) and Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) as cloud-native replacements for legacy proxies and VPNs, the San Jose company spent the period adding data security, AI security, security operations and IoT/OT controls on top of the same inline fabric that had made the original architecture commercially distinctive.

## Identity at the Snapshot Date

Zscaler, Inc. traded on Nasdaq under the ticker **ZS** and remained headquartered in **San Jose, California**. The company had been founded in 2007 by **Jay Chaudhry**, who remained Chairman and Chief Executive Officer through the frozen snapshot date. Its March 2018 initial public offering priced at **$16 a share** and raised approximately **$192 million** in gross proceeds, with the stock closing its first trading day at **$33** [IPO prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000119312518085981/d400527d424b4.htm).

## Financial Trajectory

The pace of compounding was the first fact a reader needed to hold:

| Fiscal Year (ending July 31) | Revenue | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $673.1M | — |
| FY2022 | $1.091B | +62% |
| FY2023 | $1.617B | +48% |
| FY2024 | $2.167B | +34% |
| FY2025 | $2.673B | +23% |
| FY2026 (guided, as of Feb. 26 2026) | $3.309B-$3.322B | about +24% |

*Sources: [Zscaler FY2022 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2022-financial-results), [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results), [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results), [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results), [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results)*

Annual recurring revenue crossed the **$3 billion** threshold at fiscal year-end July 2025, closing at **$3.015 billion**, up **22%** year on year [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results). By the end of the second quarter of fiscal 2026, on **31 January 2026**, ARR had expanded further to **$3.359 billion**, up **25%** year on year, while the company guided full-year FY2026 ARR to **$3.730 billion-$3.745 billion** [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results). Calculated billings in the fourth quarter of FY2025 reached **$1.202 billion**, up **32%**, while non-GAAP operating margin in Q2 FY2026 reached **22%** and quarterly free cash flow was **$169.1 million** [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results) [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

## Platform Architecture and the Expansion Thesis

The Zero Trust Exchange rested on three established pillars: **ZIA**, which replaced forward proxies and secure web gateways; **ZPA**, which replaced network-level VPN access with application-level access; and **ZDX**, which gave operations teams end-to-end visibility into user experience. By the frozen window, management was no longer framing those as the whole company. The additional economic thrust lay in cloud DLP, CASB, data security posture management, Risk360, AI security controls, and IoT/OT segmentation, all sold as extensions of the same policy and inspection layer rather than as separately deployed products [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm).

The AI inflection sharpened that expansion thesis. In the fiscal third quarter of 2025, Chaudhry said: "The proliferation of AI in all aspects of business is increasing the need for our AI security. We empower customers to securely adopt both public GenAI apps and their own private AI apps, and we are increasing our investments in this area" [Q3 FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-third-quarter-fiscal-2025-financial-results). By the February 2026 quarter, the framing had become more explicit: management said it believed Zscaler was "the cybersecurity platform for the AI age" because inline policy enforcement was already running at scale across the installed base [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

## The Acquisition Layer

Two acquisitions in the first quarter of fiscal 2026 turned that argument into disclosed assets. Zscaler completed the acquisition of **Red Canary** on **1 August 2025** [Red Canary close release](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-completes-acquisition-red-canary-accelerate-innovations). It acquired **SPLXAI Inc.** on **31 October 2025**, and in its first-quarter fiscal 2026 shareholder letter said the two acquisitions had closed during the quarter for aggregate consideration of **$692.0 million** [Q1 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2026-financial-results). By the second quarter of FY2026, management said Red Canary had contributed **$114 million of ARR**, giving Zscaler an immediate managed-detection-and-response foothold as it pushed further into agentic security operations [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

## Competitive Position and Open Questions

By the frozen date, Zscaler remained the largest pure-play zero-trust SSE vendor by revenue, but the competitive field had tightened. Palo Alto Networks pressed the consolidation argument from a firewall incumbent's installed base; Netskope remained the most direct pure-play challenge in data protection; Cisco had distribution leverage; and Cloudflare continued to push price and network-performance arguments in the mid-market. Within the frozen window, the central unresolved questions were whether the FY2025 billings reacceleration would persist, how quickly Red Canary's MDR assets would cross-sell into the installed base, and whether Zscaler's AI-security layer would deepen wallet share or merely broaden the product catalog.

---

chapters.title: From 2007 founding through 2018 IPO to multi-billion ARR platform
chapters.body:
## The Founding Conviction, 2007

By the time Jay Chaudhry incorporated Zscaler in San Jose in 2007, he had already built and sold four security companies — SecureIT, CipherTrust, CoreHarbor, and AirDefense — each one a proof that structural shifts in computing architecture created windows for new security categories. SecureIT, his first venture, was acquired by VeriSign in 1998 at a moment when organisations were just beginning to treat the public internet as an operating environment. CipherTrust, which addressed the explosion of email-borne threats, was sold to Secure Computing in 2006 for roughly $273 million. The exits made Chaudhry wealthy and, more importantly, gave him a pattern-recognition framework for identifying the next dislocation before the incumbents could defend against it.

The dislocation he identified in 2007 was categorical. Enterprise security architecture had been engineered around a fixed perimeter: traffic flowed into corporate data centres through hub-and-spoke networks, and hardware appliances — firewalls, proxies, VPN concentrators — sat at the choke points. That model presumed applications lived on-premises and that employees worked inside the perimeter. Both presumptions were dissolving simultaneously. Software-as-a-service was accelerating. Mobility was normalising. The perimeter, Chaudhry concluded, was becoming a fiction. Rather than iterate on the hardware stack, he resolved to rebuild the security function inside the cloud itself — to make the cloud the security perimeter.

The company he founded to execute that thesis was named Zscaler, a contraction of "Zenith Security." Its governing architecture would become the Zero Trust Exchange: a globally distributed cloud platform through which all user traffic would pass, inspected and enforced in the cloud rather than routed back through on-premises appliances.

## Building the Platform Before the Market Arrived

Building a globally distributed inspection fabric demanded capital before revenue could scale. Zscaler raised successive venture rounds — backed by Lightspeed Venture Partners, TPG Growth, and Google Capital (now CapitalG), among others — accumulating roughly $148 million in private funding through its pre-IPO years. The proceeds funded the expansion of what Zscaler calls its "nodes": cloud data centres distributed across every major region. By the time of its IPO, the company operated data centres across more than 100 cities globally.

ZIA launched first as a cloud-native secure web gateway; ZPA followed in 2016, replacing the corporate VPN with application-level access that eliminated lateral movement risk. Together they established Zscaler as a comprehensive zero-trust architecture vendor.

## March 2018: The IPO and the Public Market Debut

Zscaler priced its initial public offering on 15 March 2018, listing on the NASDAQ under the ticker ZS at $16 per share — the top of its indicated range. The company raised approximately $192 million in primary proceeds. On its first trading day, shares opened substantially above the offer price, closing around $33, a gain of more than 100 percent that reflected both the scarcity of pure-play cloud security assets in the public markets and investor appetite for the zero-trust narrative at a moment when high-profile breaches — Equifax, WannaCry, NotPetya — had made perimeter security's inadequacy viscerally apparent to boardrooms. The first-day market capitalisation reached roughly $4 billion, a multiple that embedded significant growth expectations into the stock from day one.

The prospectus disclosed fiscal 2018 (the year ending July 2018) revenues in the range of $190 million, growing rapidly from the preceding year. The business was subscription-SaaS in structure: annual recurring revenue, measured through billings and deferred revenue, was the operative metric, and gross margins were already running at levels consistent with scaled SaaS economics. Jay Chaudhry retained a dominant founder equity stake — a concentration of ownership that would persist through subsequent years and align his incentives tightly with long-run enterprise value creation rather than near-term financial engineering.

The IPO arrived at a particular inflection in enterprise computing: the hybrid-work transition was still years away, but cloud application adoption was already straining the hub-and-spoke network. The Covid-19 pandemic of 2020, when it arrived, would function as an enormous involuntary proof-of-concept for Zscaler's architecture. Organisations that had deployed ZPA could extend secure application access to newly remote workforces in days; those reliant on hardware VPN infrastructure faced weeks of capacity expansion and appliance procurement.

## The Hypergrowth Arc: FY2021 to FY2024

The post-pandemic revenue trajectory validated the platform's positioning. Revenue scaled from $673 million in fiscal 2021 to $2.167 billion in fiscal 2024 — a compound growth rate exceeding 47 percent annually. Non-GAAP profitability and positive free cash flow emerged by FY2023.

## Platform Expansion: 2023–2025

Zscaler's strategic narrative through 2023-2025 was defined by deliberate expansion beyond ZIA and ZPA. Data protection came first — cloud DLP and CASB enabling data governance through the existing inline inspection fabric. Zscaler Digital Experience (ZDX) addressed distributed-workforce performance monitoring. Risk360 aggregated threat signals into board-level risk quantification. IoT and operational technology security extended zero-trust enforcement to industrial and campus environments.

By the spring of 2026, Zscaler had travelled from a 2007 founding conviction about the obsolescence of the hardware perimeter to a multi-billion-dollar ARR platform with ambitions to serve as the security infrastructure layer for the AI-augmented enterprise — a trajectory that would have seemed improbable to the appliance vendors whose market it systematically displaced.

chapters.title: Zero Trust Exchange: ZIA, ZPA, ZDX, data protection, AI security operations, IoT/OT
chapters.body:
## The Zero Trust Exchange: Architecture as Strategy

By fiscal 2024, the Zero Trust Exchange had become a multi-service platform processing hundreds of billions of daily transactions across more than 150 points of presence worldwide, having evolved from a web proxy into a broad security fabric spanning internet access, private application connectivity, digital experience monitoring, data protection, AI-driven risk management, and operational technology security.

## ZIA: The Original Cloud Proxy

Zscaler Internet Access was the platform's founding product and, for years, its primary revenue engine. ZIA replaced the on-premises secure web gateway — dominated by Blue Coat, McAfee, and Symantec — with a cloud-delivered proxy intercepting all user traffic inline regardless of location. Unlike hardware gateways that forced backhauling through headquarters, ZIA routed traffic through the nearest Zscaler node.

ZIA bundled URL filtering, cloud sandboxing, a cloud-delivered firewall, DNS security, and advanced threat prevention. The consolidation play — collapsing multiple point products into a single subscription — defined Zscaler's upsell motion for the decade that followed.

## ZPA: Replacing the VPN

Zscaler Private Access attacked the VPN — whose network-level access became a liability as credential theft and ransomware spread. ZPA inverted the model: users connect to specific named applications through lightweight connectors, with no network-segment exposure. Commercially available from 2016, ZPA had grown to co-equal revenue status with ZIA by fiscal 2024.

## ZDX: Visibility Across the Distributed Enterprise

Zscaler Digital Experience, generally available from 2020 onward, addressed a downstream problem created by the cloud transition: when users reported poor application performance, IT teams could no longer rely on network operations centers monitoring on-premises infrastructure. The path from a remote laptop to a SaaS application traversed ISP networks, cloud provider backbones, and CDN layers that corporate IT neither owned nor monitored.

ZDX provided end-to-end path analysis — device health, last-mile segment quality, Zscaler node performance, and application server response time — synthesized into a per-user experience score. Because Zscaler already sat inline on all traffic, ZDX derived telemetry without requiring additional infrastructure beyond a lightweight endpoint sensor. The product addressed a tension familiar to IT operations teams: cloud architecture improved agility but degraded observability, and ZDX reclaimed some of that observability without reversing the shift to distributed work.

## Data Protection: DLP and CASB

As the Zero Trust Exchange scaled, Chaudhry identified data protection as the platform's next expansion vector. Because every byte of user traffic already transited the Zscaler cloud for ZIA and ZPA enforcement, adding inline data loss prevention required no additional deployment footprint. DLP policies could be applied to the same streams the platform was already inspecting.

Inline cloud access security broker capabilities allowed real-time inspection of SaaS traffic — blocking uploads of sensitive files to personal storage accounts while permitting traffic to sanctioned corporate instances of the same application. API-based CASB extended coverage to data at rest, enabling policy enforcement against files already stored in SharePoint, Google Drive, or Salesforce without requiring traffic redirection. Data security posture management capabilities provided visibility into cloud misconfigurations and data exposure risks, extending protection from the user-traffic layer into cloud infrastructure posture.

The suite competed directly with standalone vendors including Broadcom's Symantec DLP and Netskope's data security platform. Zscaler's distribution advantage lay in selling into ZIA and ZPA installed accounts — the data protection motion required no new infrastructure decision from a customer already routing traffic through the platform.

## AI Security Operations: Risk360 and Workload Protection

The 2024-2025 period saw Zscaler articulate a third expansion wave: AI-driven security operations and the protection of AI workloads themselves.

Risk360, introduced in fiscal 2023 and substantially expanded through fiscal 2025, aggregated signals from across the Zero Trust Exchange into a unified risk quantification layer. Where traditional security operations centers generated alert volumes that exceeded analyst capacity to triage, Risk360 translated raw signals into financial exposure estimates, expressing breach likelihood and potential impact in dollar terms. The product targeted a gap that Chaudhry described repeatedly in earnings settings: technical security teams could enumerate vulnerabilities, but C-suite executives and boards needed risk framed as financial exposure to allocate budgets rationally. Risk360 aspired to be the bridge.

The AI workload protection initiative reflected a category of exposure created by rapid enterprise adoption of large language models. Organizations deploying AI applications on cloud infrastructure faced questions the existing security stack had not been designed to answer: what data was being submitted to external LLM APIs through employee prompts; whether model outputs could be used to exfiltrate information; how AI-to-AI communications within cloud environments should be governed. Zscaler applied its inline inspection architecture to this traffic, positioning ZIA as a control plane for LLM queries from enterprise users, and extending ZPA-like segmentation to the API communications between AI services deployed within cloud environments. On the fiscal 2025 earnings cycle, Chaudhry argued consistently that every enterprise becoming an AI company faced the same infrastructure displacement moment that had originally made ZIA and ZPA necessary — the attack surface had expanded, and the legacy stack had not been built to address it.

## IoT and Operational Technology

The sixth pillar addressed a category that had remained underserved by enterprise security vendors for most of the sector's history: internet-of-things and operational technology devices. Manufacturing plants, utilities, healthcare systems, and logistics operations ran embedded devices — sensors, programmable logic controllers, building management systems, medical equipment — that were unmanaged, typically unable to host endpoint agents, and increasingly networked into the same infrastructure carrying enterprise IT traffic.

Zscaler's approach drew on the ZPA architecture. IoT and OT connectors allowed the platform to broker access to device communications without requiring software on the devices themselves. Zscaler acquired Airgap Networks in fiscal 2024, adding agentless segmentation capabilities designed specifically for operational technology environments where patching cycles were measured in years and agent deployment was operationally infeasible. The market rationale was partly defensive and partly expansionary: enterprise accounts that had deployed ZIA and ZPA for employee traffic retained an adjacent, unprotected attack surface in their plant floors and building systems. Extending Zero Trust Exchange coverage to that surface deepened per-customer economics without requiring new customer acquisition.

## Platform Economics

The aggregate picture by fiscal 2024 showed a platform growing fastest at the high end of the customer base. Zscaler reported 567 customers with annual contract value above $1 million as of fiscal year-end 2024, up from 481 the prior year — a cohort that served as the company's proxy for deep platform adoption across multiple product pillars rather than single-product deployment. The table below summarizes the competitive displacement thesis across each layer.

| Product | Category | Primary Displacement |
|---|---|---|
| ZIA | Secure web gateway / cloud firewall | Blue Coat, Palo Alto NGFW, Symantec WSS |
| ZPA | Zero Trust Network Access | Cisco AnyConnect, Pulse Secure |
| ZDX | Digital experience monitoring | ThousandEyes, Riverbed |
| Data Protection | DLP / CASB / DSPM | Broadcom DLP, Netskope |
| Risk360 | Risk quantification / SecOps | Tenable Lumin, ServiceNow SecOps |
| IoT/OT | OT network access and segmentation | Claroty, Armis |

Palo Alto Networks' Prisma SASE and Netskope represented the most direct competitive overlaps across multiple pillars simultaneously. Cisco's convergence of Umbrella and Catalyst SD-WAN leveraged an installed base that dwarfed Zscaler's customer count. Cloudflare's Zero Trust platform competed at the ZTNA and secure web gateway layer with pricing pressure that targeted Zscaler's mid-market. The architectural coherence of the Zero Trust Exchange — all inspection sharing a single inline data path, telemetry feeding back into a unified policy engine — remained the differentiator Chaudhry returned to when competitive questions arose on earnings calls. By fiscal 2024's $2.167 billion in revenue, the platform had grown from a web proxy into one of the most architecturally complete cloud security stacks in the enterprise market. Whether Zscaler could sustain the field execution required to monetize that breadth against competitors with larger installed bases and deeper distribution channels was the defining question entering the 2025-2026 period.

chapters.title: Revenue, ARR, billings, margin progression, capital structure
chapters.body:
The arithmetic of Zscaler's financial history through the frozen window showed not only scale but operating discipline. Revenue grew from **$673.1 million** in fiscal 2021 to **$2.673 billion** in fiscal 2025, while non-GAAP operating income, deferred revenue and free cash flow all expanded materially. What had begun as a fast-growing cloud-security story increasingly looked, by fiscal 2025, like a subscription platform with real balance-sheet capacity.

## Revenue Trajectory

The five fiscal years from 2021 through 2025 charted a managed deceleration from an unusually high base, the pattern more typical of a durable subscription franchise than a one-cycle demand spike.

| Fiscal Year (ending July 31) | Revenue | Year-on-Year Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2021 | $673.1M | — |
| FY2022 | $1.091B | +62% |
| FY2023 | $1.617B | +48% |
| FY2024 | $2.167B | +34% |
| FY2025 | $2.673B | +23% |

*Sources: [Zscaler FY2022 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2022-financial-results), [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results), [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results), [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results)*

The 62 per cent surge in fiscal 2022 arrived at the intersection of post-pandemic distributed-work adoption and the maturation of ZPA, which gave enterprises an application-level alternative to legacy VPN infrastructure. Fiscal 2023 then extended that scale-up to **$1.617 billion** of revenue, with fourth-quarter revenue of **$455.0 million** and ARR surpassing **$2 billion** [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results). By fiscal 2024, revenue had reached **$2.167 billion**, and by fiscal 2025 it reached **$2.673 billion**, confirming that the company was still adding substantial absolute dollars even as percentage growth normalised [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results).

## Annual Recurring Revenue and Billings

Because subscription revenue is recognised over the term of a contract, Zscaler's disclosed billings and ARR figures remained the better read-through on commercial momentum. Full-year calculated billings were **$1.481 billion** in FY2022 [FY2022 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2022-financial-results). Fourth-quarter calculated billings were **$719.3 million** in FY2023, **$910.8 million** in FY2024 and **$1.202 billion** in FY2025, corresponding to year-on-year growth rates of **38%**, **27%** and **32%** respectively [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results) [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results). The pattern mattered because it showed that billings growth had normalised from fiscal 2022's pandemic-era comparisons but had not collapsed; it reaccelerated into the FY2025 year-end quarter.

ARR followed a similarly clear staircase. Zscaler ended FY2023 with ARR above **$2.0 billion**, FY2024 with ARR above **$2.5 billion**, FY2025 at **$3.015 billion**, and the January 2026 quarter at **$3.359 billion** [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results) [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results) [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results). Deferred revenue, which represented contracted revenue not yet recognised, also expanded from **$1.095 billion** at July 2022 to **$1.440 billion** at July 2023, **$1.760 billion** at July 2024, and **$2.468 billion** at July 2025 [FY2022 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2022-financial-results) [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results) [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm).

## The March to Non-GAAP Profitability

The profitability story was also more measured than the prior draft suggested. Zscaler's operating leverage was real, but the annual margin profile disclosed by the company was lower in FY2022-FY2024 than the prior text stated.

| Fiscal Year | Non-GAAP Gross Margin | Non-GAAP Op. Margin | GAAP Op. Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | 79% | 10% | (30%) |
| FY2023 | 80% | 15% | (15%) |
| FY2024 | 81% | 20% | (6%) |
| FY2025 | 80% | 22% | (5%) |

*Sources: [Zscaler FY2022 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2022-financial-results), [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results), [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results), [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results)*

Gross-margin stability around 79-81 per cent reflected the architecture of the Zero Trust Exchange itself. Once enforcement capacity was built in a region, the marginal cost of routing additional enterprise traffic through that fabric was low relative to subscription revenue. Operating-margin expansion then came largely from scale and mix. Non-GAAP income from operations rose from **$111.6 million** in FY2022 to **$247.2 million** in FY2023, **$433.4 million** in FY2024 and **$592.0 million** in FY2025 [FY2022 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2022-financial-results) [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results) [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results). GAAP profitability remained held back by stock-based compensation, but the underlying operating trend was unmistakably upward.

## Free Cash Flow: The Subscription Engine Compounds

Free cash flow was also materially lower than the earlier draft had claimed, though still unusually strong for a company growing at Zscaler's rate.

| Fiscal Year | Free Cash Flow | FCF Margin |
|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $231.3M | 21% |
| FY2023 | $333.6M | 21% |
| FY2024 | $584.8M | 27% |
| FY2025 | $726.7M | 27% |

*Sources: [Zscaler FY2022 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2022-financial-results), [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results), [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results), [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results)*

The significance lay less in the absolute margin than in the consistency. Customers generally paid in advance for annual or multi-year subscriptions, while revenue was recognised ratably. That working-capital structure created cash inflows ahead of accounting recognition and kept free cash flow ahead of GAAP earnings. By the January 2026 quarter, free cash flow was **$169.1 million** on quarterly revenue of **$647.9 million**, indicating that the cash-generation profile remained intact even as the company integrated two acquisitions [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

## Capital Structure and Balance Sheet

The capital-structure discussion also required correction. The company did **not** disclose a fiscal-2023 share-repurchase authorisation in the cited filings. What it did disclose was a sequence of convertible-note transactions. In July 2025, Zscaler issued **$1.725 billion** principal amount of **0.00% convertible senior notes due 2028** and used part of the proceeds to repay the **$1.150 billion** principal amount of its 2025 notes at maturity [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm). At **31 July 2025**, cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments were **$3.572 billion**; by **31 January 2026** they were **$3.513 billion** [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm) [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

By the frozen window, the balance sheet therefore looked less like that of a capital-hungry growth company than that of a self-funding infrastructure platform: more than **$2.4 billion** of deferred revenue, more than **$3.5 billion** of cash and short-term investments, rising operating profitability, and free cash flow running comfortably positive even during an integration period. The financial profile had not become static; it had become investable at a different order of magnitude.

---

**Sources consulted:**

chapters.title: Multi-year trajectory through platform expansion and AI security pivot
chapters.body:
Between fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2025, Zscaler traced one of enterprise software's more instructive arcs: from hyper-growth security niche player to a $2.67 billion revenue business. Revenue grew roughly fourfold, annual recurring revenue crossed $3 billion, and non-GAAP net income reached $534.8 million in fiscal 2025.

The four-year trajectory ran through a distinct sequence of inflection points — a billion-dollar revenue crossing, an ARR doubling within two years, a measured deceleration in growth rates as the law of large numbers reasserted itself, a brief go-to-market reckoning, and ultimately a strategic reorientation toward artificial intelligence that repositioned the company not merely as a defender of enterprise infrastructure but as an operator of what Chaudhry called an AI-driven security operations platform.

## The $1 Billion Crossing: FY2022 and the Hyper-Growth Phase

Fiscal 2022, which ended 31 July 2022, established the commercial footing on which every subsequent milestone rested. Revenue reached $1.091 billion, a 62 percent increase on the prior year, crossing the symbolic billion-dollar threshold that separates growth-phase SaaS businesses from enterprise-scale platforms. The fourth quarter alone produced $318.1 million in revenue, with calculated billings of $520.4 million rising 57 percent year-over-year, and deferred revenue crossing $1 billion for the first time.

The company achieved what Chaudhry described as the "Rule of 80" — revenue growth plus operating margin reaching eighty — for both the quarter and full year.

> "We delivered outstanding results for the fourth quarter with 61% revenue growth and 57% billings growth year over year, while driving operational efficiency across the company and delivering on Rule of 80 for the quarter and for the full year."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2022 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2022](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368322000073/zs-07312022_991.htm)

The macro environment in calendar 2022 — rising interest rates, a sharp repricing of growth equities — did little to dent customer demand. Zero trust had passed from buzzword to budget-line item.

## The ARR Doubling: FY2023's Record Performance

Fiscal 2023 produced what Chaudhry characterised as the fastest ARR doubling in the company's history. Revenue grew to $1.617 billion, a 48 percent increase, and the Q4 result — $455.0 million, up 43 percent — pushed ARR past the $2 billion mark. Billings in the fourth quarter reached $719.3 million, a 38 percent year-over-year advance, while deferred revenue grew 41 percent to $1.44 billion, suggesting the subscription base was being locked in at an accelerating rate.

Non-GAAP profitability improved materially, with non-GAAP net income of $100.9 million in Q4 FY2023 compared with $36.4 million in the equivalent quarter a year earlier.

> "We concluded our fiscal year with strong top line growth and record operating profits. In less than two years, we doubled our annual recurring revenue, surpassing the $2 billion milestone."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2023 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368323000099/zs-07312023_991.htm)

> "With cyber security as a high priority, IT executives are modernizing their legacy network security with our zero-trust architecture."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2023, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2023](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368323000099/zs-07312023_991.htm)

## The Platform Investment Cycle: FY2024

Fiscal 2024 brought a deliberate deceleration in reported growth rates as Zscaler absorbed the consequences of its own scale, while simultaneously making the acquisitions and executive appointments that would define the next strategic phase. Revenue rose 34 percent to $2.167 billion. The fourth quarter produced $592.9 million in revenue — 30 percent growth — with billings of $910.8 million and ARR crossing $2.5 billion. The customer base exceeded 8,650, including roughly 35 percent of the Forbes Global 2000, and the dollar-based net retention rate held at 115 percent, indicating that existing customers continued to expand their Zscaler footprints. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments stood at $2.41 billion as of 31 July 2024, [per the FY2024 10-K filed with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368324000109/zs-20240731.htm).

The March 2024 Avalor acquisition added a security data fabric underpinning Risk360. Closing the year, Chaudhry signalled a shift toward go-to-market precision:

> "We ended a successful Fiscal 2024 with Q4 results exceeding the high end of our guidance across all metrics. I'm excited about the year ahead, as we enter Fiscal 2025 with a strong go-to-market machine and a high pace of innovation."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2024 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368324000097/zs-07312024_991.htm)

## The AI Security Pivot: FY2025 and the $3 Billion Threshold

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue ($B) | 1.091 | 1.617 | 2.167 | 2.673 |
| YoY Revenue Growth | +62% | +48% | +34% | +23% |
| ARR at year-end | — | $2.0B+ | $2.5B+ | $3.015B |
| Non-GAAP Net Income | $36.4M (Q4) | $100.9M (Q4) | $414.6M (FY) | $534.8M (FY) |
| GAAP Net Loss (FY) | — | — | ($57.7M) | ($41.5M) |

*Sources: [SEC 8-K filings, FY2022–FY2025](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001713683&type=8-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)*

Fiscal 2025 opened with a sequential improvement in go-to-market execution that Chaudhry acknowledged directly. First-quarter revenue of $628.0 million grew 26 percent, with Chaudhry noting that "growing customer engagements and strong sales execution drove a solid Q1 with all metrics exceeding our guidance." The second quarter — $648 million in revenue, 23 percent growth, ARR of $2.7 billion — carried additional signal: the cohort of customers spending more than $1 million in annual recurring revenue reached 620, up 25 percent year-over-year, a metric that indicated the platform's expansion modules were gaining traction at the large-enterprise tier.

Data protection was one of the clearest upsell vectors: net new annual contract value in that category grew more than 40 percent year-over-year, and 85 percent of customers in the $1 million ARR cohort had adopted two or more data protection modules; 65 percent had adopted three or more. Zscaler Digital Experience, the performance-monitoring pillar of the platform, produced ZDX Copilot bookings of approximately $50 million in Q2 FY2025, up 45 percent. Chaudhry framed the breadth of the platform as a structural competitive differentiator, taking aim at the Secure Access Service Edge category that several rivals had staked out:

> "We have gone far beyond SASE by pioneering our zero trust exchange. Simply put, we offer better security at lower cost."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q2 FY2025 earnings call, [March 5 2025](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2025/03/05/zscaler-zs-q2-2025-earnings-call-transcript/)

## The $5 Billion Mandate and the Platform's Third Act

The ambition behind the platform expansion was formalised in September 2024 when Zscaler appointed Adam Geller, a security product veteran, as Chief Product Officer, in a hire explicitly positioned around scaling the business to $5 billion in ARR and beyond. Chaudhry framed Geller's task as building an AI-driven security operations platform — a second architectural layer atop the Zero Trust Exchange. In the same period, the company appointed Phil Tee, a co-founder of enterprise AI monitoring businesses, as Executive Vice President of AI Innovations, and acquired SPLX, a prompt-injection and AI security technology business, to seed the AI Guard product line.

By the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, the shape of that third act was visible in operating metrics. Revenue grew 21 percent to $719.2 million, ARR crossed $3.015 billion — up 22 percent — and the company posted its highest quarterly operating margin on record, exceeding 22 percent. Chaudhry's characterisation of the demand environment reflected the degree to which AI exposure had become the defining customer anxiety:

> "Zscaler's Zero Trust and AI security solutions are imperative in today's world and are driving robust demand. We recently delivered AI Guardrails for Public and Private apps, and we are rapidly expanding our AI security portfolio to address the emerging risks of AI models and applications."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, Q4 FY2025 earnings release, [SEC 8-K, July 31 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000138/zs-07312025_991.htm)

Across four fiscal years, Zscaler had scaled from a cloud-native proxy business chiefly selling ZIA and ZPA to an integrated platform whose emerging product lines — AI security, data protection, digital experience monitoring — were by management's account growing at twice the rate of the core. Full-year non-GAAP net income reached $534.8 million against a GAAP net loss that had narrowed to $41.5 million, suggesting the operating leverage inherent in a subscription SaaS model was finally expressing itself at scale. The transition from growth-at-all-costs to growth-with-demonstrated-economics, which Chaudhry had begun signalling with the Rule of 80 commitment in fiscal 2022, had completed its first cycle — and a second, AI-inflected cycle was already underway.

---

chapters.title: Jay Chaudhry, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The Founder: From Himachal Pradesh to Silicon Valley

Jay Chaudhry's biography reads, in his own telling, as a parable about the inadequacy of perimeter security long before he gave the thesis a formal brand. He was born on **26 August 1958** in Panoh, a village in Himachal Pradesh. His biography on Zscaler's leadership page said electricity and running water did not reach the village until his teenage years, and that he walked nearly four kilometres each morning to attend school in a neighbouring village. He later earned a bachelor's degree in electronics engineering from IIT BHU Varanasi and master's degrees in industrial engineering, computer engineering and marketing from the University of Cincinnati before attending Harvard Business School's executive management programme [Jay Chaudhry biography](https://www.zscaler.com/company/leadership/jay-chaudhry). As of the frozen snapshot date, he remained Zscaler's Chairman and Chief Executive Officer and had held both posts since the company's 2007 founding [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm).

## Serial Founder: Four Exits Before Zscaler

Chaudhry had built and sold four security companies before Zscaler: SecureIT, CipherTrust, CoreHarbor and AirDefense. Zscaler's own biography materials consistently described him as a five-time entrepreneur, with Zscaler as the fifth company [Jay Chaudhry biography](https://www.zscaler.com/company/leadership/jay-chaudhry). The pattern across those ventures was consistent: identify the attack surface created by a change in computing architecture, build a product around it, then sell the company to a larger incumbent. Zscaler was the first time he tried to build the security layer for the cloud from inception rather than sell into the next incumbent cycle.

## The 2007 Founding Thesis and the 2018 IPO

The March 2018 IPO validated that architectural bet. By fiscal 2025, Chaudhry was still framing the company in milestone language tied to recurring revenue rather than simple scale:

> "We had an outstanding Q4, in which we achieved a new milestone of more than $3 billion of Annual Recurring Revenue while achieving our highest ever operating margin for a quarter."
>
> — Jay Chaudhry, [Zscaler FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results)

## The CFO Transition: Canessa to Rubin

For much of Zscaler's public life, **Remo Canessa** served as Chief Financial Officer, taking the company through the IPO and the hypergrowth years that followed. On **30 April 2025**, Zscaler disclosed that **Kevin Rubin** would succeed him. Rubin's employment with the company began on **26 May 2025**, and he assumed the title of Chief Financial Officer on **2 June 2025** [CFO appointment 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000078/zs-04302025_992.htm) [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm). His annual base salary was set at **$470,000**, with a target annual cash bonus of **$470,000** under the Employee Incentive Plan, plus equity awards approved by the compensation committee [CFO appointment 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000078/zs-04302025_992.htm). Rubin brought a recognisable operating profile: he had served as CFO of Alteryx from **April 2016 to March 2024**, including a short period as interim chief executive, and then as CFO of BetterUp before joining Zscaler [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm).

## Operating Leadership

The leadership bench visible in company disclosures by the frozen date was broader than the prior draft suggested, and it had changed during the window. **Adam Geller** joined as Chief Product Officer in **September 2024**, after serving as chief product officer and then chief executive of Exabeam; Zscaler said the hire was explicitly aimed at helping scale the company to **$5 billion in ARR and beyond** [Adam Geller appointment](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-appoints-adam-geller-chief-product-officer-help-scale). **Mike Rich** served as Chief Revenue Officer and President, Global Sales [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm). **Robert Schlossman** remained Chief Legal Officer and Secretary, the role in which he signed the company's principal SEC filings [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm). **Sunil Frida** had been appointed Chief Marketing Officer by the February 2026 quarter, giving the company a new external-facing go-to-market voice as AI security became a larger part of the story [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

One leadership change in the frozen window required a direct correction. **Raj Judge**, who had joined in May 2025 as Executive Vice President of Corporate Strategy & Ventures and a Class III director, was **no longer** part of the company by the snapshot date. Zscaler disclosed on **15 April 2026** that Judge had informed the company of his resignation as an executive officer and as a board member, effective immediately [April 15 2026 8-K](https://ir.zscaler.com/static-files/41c7fe89-38a0-47d3-8c09-6a529c515562).

## The Board

That resignation altered the board composition. The FY2025 proxy filed on **21 November 2025** described a **nine-member** board, with **seven** directors deemed independent under Nasdaq standards and Judge and Chaudhry as the two non-independent members [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm). But after Judge's resignation on **15 April 2026**, the board had effectively become an **eight-member** board with **seven independent directors** and Chaudhry as the only non-independent director in continuing service [April 15 2026 8-K](https://ir.zscaler.com/static-files/41c7fe89-38a0-47d3-8c09-6a529c515562).

| Director as of frozen date | Independence | Principal Credential |
|---|---|---|
| Jay Chaudhry | Non-independent | Chairman, Chief Executive Officer, founder |
| Andrew Brown | Independent | Long-tenured technology executive and board lead director |
| James Beer | Independent | Former CFO of Atlassian |
| Karen Blasing | Independent | Former CFO of Guidewire and audit committee chair |
| Scott Darling | Independent | President of Dell Technologies Capital |
| Charles Giancarlo | Independent | Chief executive of Pure Storage; former Cisco executive |
| Eileen Naughton | Independent | Former Google executive and human-capital leader |
| David Schneider | Independent | Former senior ServiceNow operating executive |

The proxy also clarified tenure points that mattered for governance context. **Karen Blasing** had joined in **January 2017**, **Charles Giancarlo** and **Scott Darling** in **November 2016**, **Eileen Naughton** in **September 2021**, and **James Beer** in **May 2024** [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm). That mix gave the board a relatively deep bench in software finance and go-to-market experience, but after Judge's departure it no longer had a second inside director alongside the founder.

## Ownership and Control

The ownership section also required tightening. The proxy said that, as of **1 November 2025**, Jay Chaudhry beneficially owned **26,857,608 shares**, representing **16.8%** of the outstanding stock [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm). The same table separately listed **Ajay Mangal, as trustee of The Chaudhry Family Trust U/A/D January 1, 2012**, as beneficial owner of **29,084,216 shares**, or **18.2%** [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm). The earlier draft's statement that Jay Chaudhry himself beneficially owned "approximately 38 per cent" of the company overstated what the SEC filing attributed to him personally. What the filing supported was a more careful conclusion: the Chaudhry family remained one of the company's dominant shareholder blocs, and founder influence remained structurally high even without a dual-class voting structure.

Zscaler's capital structure in the cited filings was **single-class common stock**, not the dual-class arrangement described elsewhere in the dossier. Control therefore rested on economic ownership concentration rather than super-voting shares. That distinction mattered because it made the governance story less extreme than a founder-controlled dual-class company, but still tighter than a widely dispersed software issuer.

---

*Sources: [Zscaler FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm) · [Zscaler FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm) · [Zscaler CFO appointment 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000078/zs-04302025_992.htm) · [Raj Judge resignation 8-K](https://ir.zscaler.com/static-files/41c7fe89-38a0-47d3-8c09-6a529c515562) · [Jay Chaudhry biography](https://www.zscaler.com/company/leadership/jay-chaudhry) · [Adam Geller appointment](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-appoints-adam-geller-chief-product-officer-help-scale) · [Zscaler Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results)

chapters.title: Enterprise, federal, partner channel, go-to-market motion
chapters.body:
## Enterprise Customer Architecture

Zscaler built its commercial engine around a deliberately concentrated targeting strategy: sell the Global 2000 on replacing the network-security perimeter not with newer boxes, but with a cloud-delivered control plane. By the frozen window, that motion had produced a customer base that was both large and increasingly skewed toward high-value relationships. The company reported **8,650 customers** at fiscal year-end 2024 and **more than 9,400 customers** at fiscal year-end 2025, with nearly **40% of the Forbes Global 2000** and **45% of the Fortune 500** as customers by the latter date [FY2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368324000109/zs-20240731.htm) [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results).

The consequences of that strategy were most legible in the large-account cohorts management highlighted in company-posted earnings commentary:

| Period | Total customers | Customers generating >$1M in ARR | Other cohort detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 FY2024 | about 8,000 | 468 | nearly 2,700 customers >$100K ARR |
| FY2024 year-end | 8,650 | 567 | more than 60 customers >$5M ARR |
| Q2 FY2025 | not separately restated | 620 | 3,000 customers >$100K ARR |
| FY2025 year-end | more than 9,400 | 664 | nearly 40% of Forbes Global 2000 |
| Q1 FY2026 | not separately restated | 698 | 3,754 customers >$100K ARR |

*Sources: [Q1 FY2024 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2024-financial-results), [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results), [Q2 FY2025 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/static-files/ef251943-fc84-4c7f-a6c7-829d102d4b5b), [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results), [Q1 FY2026 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/static-files/feb0f451-db2a-48f5-9fc9-8de1c03ed292)*

That widening gap between total customers and seven-figure customers was the real commercial signal. It suggested that Zscaler was not simply adding logos; it was graduating customers into broader platform relationships. Management repeatedly tied that dynamic to multi-pillar adoption rather than to pricing alone. In the fiscal first quarter of 2024, for example, Chaudhry said nearly half of all new logos had adopted the company's "three user pillars" of ZIA, ZPA and ZDX from the outset [Q1 FY2024 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2024-financial-results).

## The Federal Beachhead

The federal motion was also better documented than the earlier draft implied. The policy foundation came from **Executive Order 14028**, issued on **12 May 2021**, which directed agencies to strengthen zero-trust architecture and federal cybersecurity practices [White House EO 14028](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/05/12/executive-order-on-improving-the-nations-cybersecurity/). The Office of Management and Budget then set a more specific implementation path in memorandum **M-22-09**, "Moving the U.S. Government Toward Zero Trust Cybersecurity Principles" [OMB M-22-09](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/M-22-09.pdf).

Zscaler's product eligibility inside that policy framework was not a vague claim. The FedRAMP marketplace listed **Zscaler Internet Access** and **Zscaler Private Access** at the **FedRAMP High** baseline, and the company said more than **100 federal agencies and federal systems integrators** were using Zscaler solutions [FedRAMP marketplace](https://marketplace.fedramp.gov/products/FR1831334858) [FedRAMP marketplace](https://marketplace.fedramp.gov/products/FR1839869370). In the fiscal first quarter of 2024, management disclosed a **record U.S. federal quarter**, with new federal business up **more than 90% year on year** and four federal deals above **$1 million** in annual contract value [Q1 FY2024 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2024-financial-results). By the fiscal first quarter of 2026, the company had also launched **FedRAMP Moderate**-authorised cloud data centres in **London** and **Paris**, signalling that the public-sector playbook was being exported to allied-government and sovereign-data contexts beyond the United States [Q1 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2026-financial-results).

## Partner Channel Architecture

The partner layer was likewise more specific in primary disclosures than the prior draft suggested. In its FY2025 10-K, Zscaler identified representative channel partners that included telecommunications providers such as **BT**, **Deutsche Telekom**, **Orange Business** and **Verizon**, as well as system integrators such as **Deloitte LLP** and **HCL America**, alongside a broader group of value-added resellers and managed service providers [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm). Those relationships mattered because the architecture was often sold not as a point product but as the security layer within a larger cloud and network redesign.

Management's own deal commentary showed that point in action. On the fiscal first quarter 2024 call, Chaudhry highlighted a large transformation project led by **Accenture** in which the customer selected Zscaler over the incumbent firewall stack after piloting the platform [Q1 FY2024 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2024-financial-results). Near the end of the frozen window, Zscaler also announced **Project AI-Guardian**, a partner programme with **Tata Consultancy Services** and **Wipro** focused on secure enterprise AI adoption, evidence that the channel story had extended from zero-trust migration into AI-governance workstreams [Project AI-Guardian](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-launches-project-ai-guardian-partners-tcs-and-wipro).

Managed service providers formed a distinct channel layer rather than a footnote to the direct sales force. For customers without mature internal security operations teams, those partners turned Zscaler from a software subscription into an operated service. The result was that the partner programme did not merely widen distribution below Zscaler's direct-sales ceiling; it also reduced friction in complex migrations where a systems integrator or telecom carrier already controlled the customer relationship.

## Net Retention and the Land-and-Expand Engine

The retention story also needed tightening. Zscaler had **not** maintained disclosure of net revenue retention "in excess of 120%" throughout its public life. Instead, the company disclosed **120%** dollar-based net retention in Q1 FY2024, **115%** in Q2 FY2025, and **114%** in both Q3 FY2025 and FY2025 year-end commentary [Q1 FY2024 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [Q2 FY2025 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/static-files/ef251943-fc84-4c7f-a6c7-829d102d4b5b) [Q3 FY2025 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-third-quarter-fiscal-2025-financial-results) [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results). The important point was not that retention remained above an arbitrary threshold forever; it was that even after normalisation it remained comfortably above 100%, meaning the installed base still expanded faster than it churned.

That land-and-expand motion was inseparable from product sequence. Customers typically entered through ZIA or ZPA, validated the architecture, and then layered on ZDX, data protection, segmentation or AI-security modules. Management's disclosures on large-customer cohorts effectively served as a proxy for platform depth, because the company did not break out revenue by product family in its SEC filings. The larger the million-dollar cohort became, the stronger the evidence that Zscaler was being bought as architecture rather than as a single-feature swap.

## Go-to-Market Evolution Into the AI Era

As fiscal 2025 gave way to fiscal 2026, the go-to-market motion increasingly centred on AI-related risk. The pitch was not that AI would replace the earlier zero-trust thesis; it was that employee use of public large-language-model tools, private AI apps and agentic workflows created precisely the sort of inline data-governance problem the Zero Trust Exchange had been built to solve. By the Q2 FY2026 quarter, management was explicitly framing the company as a platform for securing AI and agentic workflows at scale [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

The commercial advantage in that shift was incumbency. Zscaler did not need to persuade a customer to deploy a new inspection fabric from scratch before selling AI controls; in many large accounts the traffic path was already there. That is why the company kept emphasising its expanding large-customer cohorts, its federal traction and its partner ecosystem together. They were different disclosures describing the same underlying fact: by the frozen date, Zscaler's sales motion was no longer simply a new-logo story. It was an installed-base monetisation story with AI as the newest catalyst.

---
