chapters.title: Where Zscaler sits against Palo Alto Prisma, Netskope, Cisco, Cloudflare
chapters.body:
By the time Zscaler's annual recurring revenue crossed $3 billion in mid-fiscal 2025, the company had spent nearly two decades arguing a single architectural proposition: that security should live in the cloud, inline between users and applications, rather than in hardware stacked in corporate data centres. That proposition was, by the spring of 2026, no longer controversial. It had become the organising thesis of the entire enterprise security market — which meant every major vendor in that market was now competing directly with Zscaler.

The competitive field that formed around Zscaler was varied in origin but convergent in ambition. Palo Alto Networks attacked from the established security incumbency, leveraging its dominant firewall franchise and a $6.33 billion Next-Generation Security ARR base to assemble a rival SASE platform. Netskope, a cloud-native proxy pure-play that finally reached public markets in September 2025, contested the same blue-chip enterprise logos with differentiated data-loss prevention. Cisco brought its vast installed networking base and bundling leverage — and the sales reach of 60,000-plus enterprise relationships. Cloudflare arrived from a different direction entirely, building zero-trust access on top of a global content-delivery network that already touched the internet at scale. And behind those four principals, a longer tail of vendors — Forcepoint, Skyhigh Security, Check Point Harmony SASE, Lookout — competed for mid-market share and specialised verticals.

## The Principal Rival: Palo Alto Networks Prisma

No competitive pairing drew more analyst attention through 2025 and into 2026 than Zscaler versus Palo Alto Networks. The two companies had roughly comparable revenues — Zscaler reported $2.673 billion for fiscal year 2025 against Palo Alto's full-year guidance of $11.3 billion, though Palo Alto's total included network security, cloud security, and a large on-premises installed base — but in the specific SASE/SSE contest, the numbers converged more closely. Palo Alto's SASE ARR reached $1.5 billion in the fiscal second quarter of 2026, growing approximately 40 per cent year-on-year, against Zscaler's total company ARR of $3.4 billion growing 25 per cent. The two vendors were, in market-analyst parlance, trading at different multiples on different base sizes, but both were compounding faster than the broader security market.

| Vendor | ARR / NGS ARR (most recent Q) | YoY Growth | Gartner MQ Position |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zscaler | $3.4B (Q2 FY2026, Jan 2026) | +25% | SSE Leader (1st) |
| Palo Alto SASE only | $1.5B (Q2 FY2026, Jan 2026) | ~+40% | SASE / SSE / SD-WAN Leader |
| Netskope | $754M ARR (Q3 FY2026, Oct 2025) | +34% | SSE Leader / Forrester highest |
| Cloudflare | ~$2.4B total rev. run-rate | +31–34% | SASE Visionary |

Palo Alto's competitive pitch rested on two pillars: breadth and depth. Its Prisma Access platform carried the full Layer 7 inspection capability of a next-generation firewall into the cloud, offering packet-level visibility that Palo Alto's marketing teams positioned as superior to what they called Zscaler's "proxy-overlay" approach. Prisma Browser added a natively integrated enterprise browser — serving more than 1,500 enterprise customers with over nine million licences by early 2026 — a capability Zscaler did not match organically, though the company moved to address the gap through its acquisition of browser-security startup SquareX. Palo Alto was, critically, the only vendor recognised as a Gartner Magic Quadrant leader in all three adjacent categories simultaneously: SASE, SSE, and SD-WAN, a distinction its sales teams weaponised in competitive evaluations. The company's [second-quarter FY2026 investor materials](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/palo-alto-networks-q2-2026-slides-ngs-arr-jumps-33-stock-falls-5-93CH-4511827) showed 1,100-plus "platformized" customers — accounts that had consolidated four or more Palo Alto product families — as evidence that the consolidation trade was going its way.

## Architecture as the Core Argument

Against Palo Alto's firepower, Zscaler returned again and again to architecture. The company's Zero Trust Exchange, built cloud-natively from its 2007 founding rather than cloudified from hardware, operated across more than 150 points of presence and 160 data centres globally by 2025, processing hundreds of billions of transactions per day in-line between users and destinations. The distinction mattered technically: a proxy-based inline model meant Zscaler could inspect, modify, and enforce policy on every byte of traffic traversing its platform, creating a telemetry reservoir that improved machine-learning models in a self-reinforcing loop. The scale of that reservoir — accumulated over eighteen years of cloud-only operation — was not easily replicated.

Jay Chaudhry framed the architectural bet in terms of the AI transition on Zscaler's first-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings call:

> "The best AI security is built on the foundation of Zero Trust."

And on the company's second-quarter call, as the proliferation of AI agents became the dominant enterprise-security narrative:

> "Enterprises will need 'inline policy enforcement at massive scale' as AI agents proliferate."

Zscaler's position was that Palo Alto's NGFW-in-the-cloud approach, however capable, was a different animal — a security inspection appliance delivered as a service rather than a purpose-built cloud fabric. Customers running Prisma Access still typically paired it with a third-party SD-WAN vendor, or with Palo Alto's own Prisma SD-WAN, adding integration complexity. Zscaler, by contrast, had always required no WAN hardware at the edge, and its [Zero Trust Branch](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2026-financial-results) segmentation product — introduced to isolate branch networks without traditional firewalls — extended that no-hardware premise further into campus and industrial environments.

## Netskope: The Pure-Play Challenger

Netskope occupied a narrower but genuine threat. The San Jose-based vendor filed for its initial public offering in August 2025, disclosing $707 million in ARR, growing 33 per cent year-on-year, and completed the offering in September at $19 per share, raising approximately $908 million. By the third fiscal quarter of 2026, ARR had reached $754 million, and the company reported a dollar-based net retention rate of 118 per cent against a base of roughly 4,300 customers, more than 100 of whom paid in excess of $1 million annually.

Netskope's differentiation centred on data security. Its inline Data Loss Prevention and Cloud Access Security Broker capabilities were consistently rated superior to Zscaler's by enterprise security teams in proof-of-concept evaluations, particularly in regulated industries where granular data classification mattered. Forrester's 2025 SASE Wave awarded Netskope the highest composite score among all vendors, ahead of Palo Alto and Zscaler, a recognition that carried weight in accounts where DLP was the primary buying criterion. The company had not, however, resolved its profitability challenge: full-year net losses reached $354.5 million in fiscal 2025, up from $344.9 million the prior year, a trajectory that post-IPO public-market investors would scrutinise closely. Zscaler, by contrast, had been generating positive non-GAAP operating income since fiscal 2020.

## Cisco: The Incumbent Bundler

Cisco's competitive relevance rested less on architectural innovation than on distribution leverage. The company's Cisco+ Secure Connect Now combined Meraki SD-WAN with Umbrella's Secure Service Edge capabilities into a single-vendor SASE offer — directly targeting the large installed base of enterprises already running Meraki campus switches and Catalyst SD-WAN across their branch networks. With more than 60,000 enterprise relationships worldwide and a global sales organisation that dwarfed any pure-play security vendor's, Cisco could attach security subscriptions to hardware refresh cycles in ways Zscaler, Netskope, or Cloudflare could not.

The financial picture, however, was complicated. Cisco's security segment grew 59 per cent in fiscal 2025, a figure inflated by the March 2024 acquisition of Splunk; stripped of that contribution, the underlying security business faced more modest growth, and by Q1 fiscal 2026 the security segment had turned negative year-on-year, declining 2 per cent. Enterprise buyers increasingly distinguished between Cisco's networking-rooted security stack — perceived as stitched-together from Umbrella, Duo, and Meraki acquisitions — and the architecturally coherent platforms of Zscaler or even Palo Alto. [Dell'Oro Group research](https://www.channelfutures.com/sdn-sd-wan/zscaler-palo-alto-networks-cisco-sase-market) identified Palo Alto, Cisco, and Zscaler as the top three vendors in SASE by revenue, but the gap between Cisco's legacy revenue and its cloud-native SASE bookings reflected a transition that remained incomplete.

## Cloudflare and the Network-Centric Insurgents

Cloudflare represented a qualitatively different threat: a vendor approaching zero-trust from the network infrastructure layer rather than from security inspection. Its Cloudflare One platform — combining ZTNA, SWG, CASB, and remote browser isolation — ran on the same global network that already handled a meaningful fraction of the internet's DNS and CDN traffic, giving it inherent performance advantages in latency-sensitive geographies. The company [reported](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/cloudflare-q1-2026-slides-34-revenue-growth-large-customer-base-surges-93CH-4671018) 34 per cent revenue growth in Q1 2026 and signed what management described as the company's longest SASE contract during the first quarter of 2025. Gartner's 2025 SASE Magic Quadrant classified Cloudflare as a Visionary rather than a Leader — reflecting a platform that was still maturing in enterprise DLP and advanced threat-prevention depth — but the trajectory was upward. BTIG's late-2025 decision to downgrade Zscaler to Neutral, citing "intensifying zero-trust competition," specifically named Cloudflare alongside Netskope as the sources of incremental competitive pressure in the small-to-mid enterprise segment.

## The Longer Tail

Beyond the four principals, a second tier of vendors competed for specific verticals and mid-market accounts. Check Point's Harmony SASE — rebranded and extended to include an enterprise browser in 2025 — earned a strong threat-prevention score in Miercom's 2025 benchmark and appealed to enterprises already standardised on Check Point's firewall estate. Forcepoint and Skyhigh Security (formerly McAfee Enterprise's cloud business, operating under Musarubra/Skyhigh's private-equity ownership) maintained loyal installed bases in data-centric verticals, particularly US federal government and financial services, where policy compliance requirements made their specialised DLP heritage compelling. Lookout served the mobile-centric SSE segment.

None of these vendors individually posed a systemic threat to Zscaler's enterprise motion, but collectively they ensured that competitive intensity across the full market remained high, compression on average selling prices remained a structural reality, and the number of evaluation criteria against which Zscaler had to defend continued to expand.

## The Structural Moat

Zscaler's most durable competitive asset was not any single product but the architecture itself — and the eighteen years of operational data that had accumulated inside it. Every transaction inspected, every policy enforced, every threat blocked added signal to the Zero Trust Exchange's machine-learning models. By early 2026 the company processed hundreds of billions of daily transactions across its global fabric; Chaudhry cited the company as well positioned to surpass $10 billion in ARR over the longer term, implying a belief that the Exchange's data-gravity advantage would compound faster than rivals could replicate it through platform assembly.

That thesis was coherent, though not without stress points. Palo Alto's NGS ARR trajectory — targeting $20 billion by 2030 on the back of its platformization strategy — and Netskope's DLP depth represented genuine architectural challenges to specific Zscaler customer segments. The market itself was growing fast enough — the SSE segment alone was projected by Grand View Research to expand at a 21.9 per cent compound annual rate from $6.26 billion in 2024 to $36.87 billion by 2033 — that multiple vendors could compound simultaneously without fighting purely zero-sum battles. But the platform consolidation pressure that had shrunk the long tail of point-product security vendors in the early 2020s was now pressing on the SASE layer itself. By May 2026, the question for Zscaler was not whether its architecture was sound, but whether it could expand broadly enough — into data security, AI operations, IoT segmentation, and managed detection — to remain the centre of gravity around which customers consolidated, rather than one pillar among many inside a larger Palo Alto or Cisco bundle.

---

*Sources: [Zscaler Q2 FY2026 earnings highlights](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/zscaler-q2-earnings-call-highlights-231716045.html) · [Zscaler Q1 FY2026 earnings transcript](https://www.investing.com/news/transcripts/earnings-call-transcript-zscaler-beats-q1-2026-expectations-stock-rises-93CH-4378556) · [Zscaler FY2025 10-K via SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm) · [Palo Alto Q2 FY2026 SASE ARR $1.5B](https://www.ainvest.com/news/palo-alto-platformization-payoff-30-3-margin-1-5b-sase-arr-2602/) · [Palo Alto FY2026 revenue outlook $11.3B](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/palo-alto-networks-lifts-fy2026-182652208.html) · [Netskope Q3 FY2026 results](https://www.netskope.com/press-releases/netskope-announces-strong-third-quarter-fiscal-year-2026-financial-results) · [Netskope S-1 SEC filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0002063196/000095017025110855/ck0002063196-20250822.htm) · [Netskope IPO 8-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0002063196/000119312525315967/ck0002063196-ex99_1.htm) · [Cloudflare Q1 2026 results](https://www.investing.com/news/company-news/cloudflare-q1-2026-slides-34-revenue-growth-large-customer-base-surges-93CH-4671018) · [Zscaler/PANW/Cisco SASE market — Channel Futures](https://www.channelfutures.com/sdn-sd-wan/zscaler-palo-alto-networks-cisco-sase-market) · [Gartner SASE rankings — SDxCentral](https://www.sdxcentral.com/news/netskope-palo-alto-networks-zscaler-lead-forrester-sase-rankings/) · [Grand View SSE market forecast](https://www.grandviewresearch.com/industry-analysis/security-service-edge-sse-market-report)*

chapters.title: Timeline from 2007 founding through 2018 IPO and platform expansion
chapters.body:
## The Founding Thesis Validated

The Zero Trust Exchange that Chaudhry launched in 2007 — ZIA for secure web access, ZPA for private application access — became the vendor most closely identified with zero-trust delivery at enterprise scale.

## The 2018 IPO

The March 2018 IPO at $16 per share raised $192 million; first-day gains of 106% signalled investor appetite for the zero-trust thesis.

## Post-IPO Scaling and the COVID Inflection

COVID-19 accelerated the thesis. Enterprise teams compelled to support remote workforces in March 2020 drove sharp ZPA demand. Revenue scaled from $673M in fiscal 2021 to $2.167B in fiscal 2024.

## Platform Expansion

By fiscal 2023-2024, the narrative shifted toward platform breadth: ZDX for digital experience monitoring, cloud DLP and CASB for data protection, Risk360 for board-level risk quantification.

## Federal and Channel Traction

FedRAMP High authorization positioned Zscaler for US federal adoption; channel-sourced deals through SIs and MSSPs carried an increasing share of bookings.

## AI Security Operations: The 2024–2026 Catalyst

From fiscal 2024 forward, Chaudhry positioned AI as both threat surface and operational capability. Generative AI created data-leakage risk through LLM endpoints; Zscaler's inline architecture was structurally positioned to govern that traffic. IoT/OT security extended zero-trust to factory floors and building systems. Each expansion module enlarged per-customer contract value, driving net revenue retention above 100%.

chapters.title: Cloud-native architecture IP, zero-trust patents, R&D framework
chapters.body:
The 2007 decision to build a multi-tenant, cloud-native proxy rather than software tied to physical appliances embedded a durable IP position into the platform. By the frozen window, management said Zscaler was processing **more than 500 billion requests a day** across **more than 160 data centres globally**, a scale claim the company used repeatedly to argue that threat-detection data and policy telemetry compounded into a competitive asset rather than just an operating statistic [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results). ZPA's inside-out connectivity model, in which applications established outbound-only connectivity through connectors rather than exposing listening ports to the public internet, remained central to the company's zero-trust networking patents and its broader claim that architecture itself was the moat.

## Patent Portfolio: Six Domains, Seventeen Years

The patent-count discussion also needed updating to the latest disclosure in the frozen window. As of **31 July 2025**, Zscaler's FY2025 10-K said the company held **more than 725 issued patents and pending patent applications** in the United States and internationally, including **more than 325 issued patents** [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm). The earlier FY2024 figure of more than 580 applications and patents, including more than 260 issued patents, was no longer the most recent disclosure. The portfolio stretched from early cloud-proxy claims such as U.S. Patent **7,894,350** to newer grants aligned with security operations and AI-security workflows, and the public patent registry showed issue and expiry dates extending into the 2040s [Zscaler patent registry](https://www.zscaler.com/legal/patents).

The company's public registry organised that portfolio into six product-aligned domains:

| Patent Category | Associated Products | Scale |
|---|---|---|
| Cloud Protection | ZIA, Zero Trust Exchange, Posture Control, Workload Communications | 85+ patents |
| Zero Trust Networking | ZIA, ZPA, Zero Trust Branch, Zero Trust Browser | 60+ patents |
| Data Protection | Enterprise DLP, CASB, DSPM, Cloud Browser Isolation | 60+ patents |
| Cyber Threat Protection | ThreatLabz, ATP, Cloud Sandbox, Cloud Firewall, Cloud IPS | growing |
| Security Operations | Agentic SecOps, Deception, Unified Vulnerability Management | growing |
| Digital Experience & AI Security | ZDX, AI-powered segmentation, AI red teaming, AI Protect | growing |

Cloud Protection remained the deepest tranche, reflecting the foundational nature of the inline proxy and cloud-delivered policy architecture. Zscaler supplemented the patent estate with copyright, trademark and trade-secret protections, a standard formulation repeated in its 10-K filings but meaningful in the context of a platform that depended on proprietary traffic-inspection logic and telemetry models [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm).

## R&D Investment Trajectory

Zscaler continued to fund engineering at a rate above the software-sector median, treating the cost base as competitive investment rather than overhead. The company's disclosed R&D expense was **$289.3 million** in FY2022, **$349.5 million** in FY2023, **$499.8 million** in FY2024 and **$672.6 million** in FY2025, equivalent to roughly **26.5%**, **21.6%**, **23.1%** and **25.2%** of revenue respectively [FY2022 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368322000096/zs-20220731.htm) [FY2023 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368323000117/zs-20230731.htm) [FY2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368324000109/zs-20240731.htm) [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm).

The step-up from FY2024 to FY2025 reflected both organic headcount growth and acquisition integration. Zscaler's filings identified principal engineering locations in San Jose, India, Canada, Israel and Spain, a footprint designed to keep product development running across time zones and specialised technical domains [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm).

## Acquisitions Filling Capability Gaps

The acquisition record also needed tightening. **Canonic Security** was acquired in **February 2023**, adding SaaS application security posture management [Canonic acquisition](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-acquires-canonic-security-expand-data-protection-and). **Avalor** was acquired in **February 2024**, and Zscaler used it as the engineering foundation for Risk360; the FY2024 10-K disclosed **$28.7 million** of developed technology and **$95.5 million** of goodwill from the deal rather than the purchase-price shorthand cited in the earlier draft [FY2024 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368324000109/zs-20240731.htm). **Airgap Networks** was announced in **April 2024**, not fiscal 2023, and supplied the agentless segmentation technology Zscaler later used in its IoT/OT and Zero Trust Branch push [Airgap acquisition](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-acquires-airgap-networks-expand-zero-trust-branch-and).

By the frozen window, the acquisition cadence had extended into AI security and security operations through **Red Canary** and **SPLXAI**, but the pattern remained consistent: Zscaler bought narrow capabilities that could be inserted into the larger Zero Trust Exchange rather than buying adjacent platforms that would remain operationally separate [Q1 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2026-financial-results).

## AI as the Next Defensible Layer

Through fiscal 2024 and 2025, Zscaler positioned AI less as marketing garnish than as the next defensible layer on top of data scale. Processing more than 500 billion requests a day created a training corpus unavailable to vendors without comparable traffic density, while the company's AI security products targeted prompt injection, sensitive-data leakage and policy control around both public and private AI applications. Chaudhry said in the fiscal third quarter of 2025 that the proliferation of AI across business workflows was increasing the need for Zscaler's AI security and that the company was raising its investment accordingly [Q3 FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-third-quarter-fiscal-2025-financial-results).

The R&D framework that emerged by the frozen date therefore combined sustained above-median spending, a geographically distributed engineering base, targeted tuck-in acquisitions and a patent estate that had grown meaningfully even in the twelve months between the FY2024 and FY2025 10-Ks. The underlying point survived the fact-check intact: Zscaler's product strategy was inseparable from a long-duration investment programme in architecture and IP. What changed in the corrected version was the scale and timing of the disclosed facts.

chapters.body:
## The Risk Ledger

The same forces that elevated Zscaler into a multi-billion-dollar subscription franchise also produced a distinctive risk profile. By the frozen window, those risks clustered around competitive pressure, the arithmetic of growth normalisation, foreign-exchange and macro sensitivity in an increasingly international book of business, regulatory fragmentation across jurisdictions, elongated enterprise buying cycles and governance concentration around the founder.

## Competitive Intensity

The competitive landscape in 2025 and early 2026 was more crowded than at any point since the 2018 IPO. Palo Alto Networks pushed platform consolidation across firewall, cloud and SASE budgets. Netskope remained aggressive in data protection. Cisco brought bundling leverage through networking estates already inside enterprise branches. Cloudflare kept pressing the network-performance and price argument. Zscaler's answer was not to retreat to the ZIA/ZPA core but to broaden the product set into ZDX, Risk360, AI security, Zero Trust Branch and managed detection. That strategy made commercial sense, but it also ensured the company would be fighting more competitors in more categories at once.

## Billings Growth Normalization

The mathematical consequence of a larger revenue base was unavoidable moderation in percentage growth. But the corrected numbers showed that the story was not a straight line of decline. Fourth-quarter calculated billings growth was **57%** in FY2022 on **$520.4 million** of billings, **38%** in FY2023 on **$719.3 million**, **27%** in FY2024 on **$910.8 million**, and then **32%** in FY2025 on **$1.202 billion** [FY2022 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2022-financial-results) [FY2023 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2023-financial-results) [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results). The risk, then, was less a simple decay curve than quarter-to-quarter volatility around a still-large base. That left little room for execution slippage when investors were anchoring on billings as a leading indicator.

## Foreign Exchange and International Revenue Mix

Zscaler's filings did support the broader point that international expansion created additional macro sensitivity. The FY2025 10-K said the company generated revenue in multiple countries, incurred operating expenses in foreign currencies and used foreign-currency forward contracts to hedge selected exposures [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm). The company's contracts were still largely denominated in U.S. dollars, which meant the immediate accounting risk was not pure translation. The more important commercial risk lay in local-currency affordability: a strong dollar made Zscaler more expensive relative to local budgets and, in some geographies, relative to competitors with a different cost base or bundling model.

## Geopolitical and Regulatory Fragmentation

The geopolitical environment around cybersecurity software also grew more complex. The European Union's **NIS2 Directive** raised the bar for incident reporting and supply-chain scrutiny across critical infrastructure operators, creating a combination of demand opportunity and procurement friction for U.S.-headquartered vendors [NIS2 directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2555/oj). Data residency and sovereign-cloud concerns in Europe did not invalidate Zscaler's architecture, but they did extend deal cycles and increase legal review in sensitive sectors. In the United States, federal zero-trust mandates created tailwinds for the company's public-sector business, but they also made accreditation and operational assurance non-negotiable [White House EO 14028](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/05/12/executive-order-on-improving-the-nations-cybersecurity/) [OMB M-22-09](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/M-22-09.pdf).

## Enterprise Sales Cycle Elongation

Management commentary during the frozen window supported a more measured version of the sales-cycle risk than the earlier draft used. In the fiscal first quarter of 2024, Chaudhry said the company was still seeing **elevated scrutiny of large deals**, though conditions were improving at the margin [Q1 FY2024 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2024-financial-results). In the fiscal third quarter of 2025, he again pointed to **better sales execution** and robust demand, wording that implied scrutiny had not disappeared even as conversion improved [Q3 FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-third-quarter-fiscal-2025-financial-results). For a company whose transformational deployments could replace firewalls, VPN concentrators and parts of the WAN stack at once, elongated approval chains remained a structural hazard. A delayed deal was often a deal reopened to competition.

## Governance and Founder Concentration

The governance section required a material correction. The cited SEC filings did **not** describe Zscaler as a dual-class company with Class B super-voting shares. The company had a **single class of common stock** outstanding in the cited proxy and 10-K materials [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm) [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000158/zs-20250731.htm). As of **1 November 2025**, Jay Chaudhry beneficially owned **26,857,608 shares**, or **16.8%** of the company, while the Chaudhry Family Trust, reported separately through trustee Ajay Mangal, held **29,084,216 shares**, or **18.2%** [FY2025 proxy](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1713683/000171368325000198/zs-20251121.htm).

That still left founder-family influence unusually high for a public software company, but it was influence created by concentrated economic ownership rather than by super-voting stock. The distinction narrowed, but did not eliminate, the governance risk. Minority shareholders were not facing a classic dual-class structure; they were facing a founder with substantial ownership, long board tenure and considerable practical influence over strategic direction. Raj Judge's resignation in April 2026 also meant the board no longer had a second inside director alongside Chaudhry, reducing internal management representation at the board level while leaving founder influence intact [April 15 2026 8-K](https://ir.zscaler.com/static-files/41c7fe89-38a0-47d3-8c09-6a529c515562).

---

chapters.body:
## Standing at the Inflection

By the frozen window, the relevant baseline for Zscaler was no longer fiscal 2024 alone. The company had already reported **$2.673 billion** of FY2025 revenue, **$3.015 billion** of ARR at July 2025 year-end, and guidance for **$3.309 billion-$3.322 billion** of FY2026 revenue after the January 2026 quarter [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results) [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results). Jay Chaudhry's task was therefore no longer to prove that zero trust could become a public-company category. It was to show that the Zero Trust Exchange could keep broadening into data security, AI security and security operations without losing architectural coherence.

## AI Security: Threat Vector and Product Category

Generative AI created a new exfiltration surface: employees submitting sensitive data to public LLM endpoints and enterprises wiring internal systems into private AI apps and agentic workflows. Zscaler's pitch in the frozen window was that these traffic patterns still ran through the same inline control layer it already operated at scale. Management said in February 2026 that the company was uniquely positioned to secure the "speed and scale of AI and agentic workflows" because policy enforcement was already happening in-line rather than on an after-the-fact monitoring layer [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results).

## Federal Scaling

The U.S. federal market remained one of the most important non-commercial runways. The policy case came from Executive Order 14028 and OMB memorandum M-22-09, which pushed agencies toward zero-trust implementation [White House EO 14028](https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/05/12/executive-order-on-improving-the-nations-cybersecurity/) [OMB M-22-09](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/01/M-22-09.pdf). The commercial case came from Zscaler's own disclosures: a record federal quarter in Q1 FY2024, FedRAMP High authorisations for core products, and more than 100 federal agencies and systems integrators using Zscaler solutions [Q1 FY2024 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [FedRAMP marketplace: ZIA](https://marketplace.fedramp.gov/products/FR1831334858) [FedRAMP marketplace: ZPA](https://marketplace.fedramp.gov/products/FR1839869370).

## Platform Economics

The corrected retention and cohort data still supported the central economic thesis, but with more precision. Dollar-based net retention was **120%** in Q1 FY2024, **115%** in Q2 FY2025 and **114%** by FY2025 year-end, while the cohort of customers generating more than **$1 million in ARR** expanded from **567** at FY2024 year-end to **664** at FY2025 year-end and **698** by Q1 FY2026 [Q1 FY2024 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-first-quarter-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [FY2024 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2024-financial-results) [Q2 FY2025 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/static-files/ef251943-fc84-4c7f-a6c7-829d102d4b5b) [FY2025 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-reports-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-financial-results) [Q1 FY2026 commentary](https://ir.zscaler.com/static-files/feb0f451-db2a-48f5-9fc9-8de1c03ed292). That was still a land-and-expand engine. It was simply a more mature one than the earlier draft implied.

## Competitive Posture

Zscaler's structural defence rested on two disclosed assets: a global cloud fabric of **more than 160 data centres** and a telemetry base of **more than 500 billion requests per day** [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results). Threat intelligence and policy tuning improved with scale, which made the platform harder to replicate than a conventional product catalog. The risk was that buyers might still prefer broader bundles from Palo Alto, Cisco or Microsoft even if Zscaler's architecture remained purer.

## The 2026-2030 Horizon

The forward case at the frozen date rested on a simple but still defensible proposition: Zscaler had not exhausted the original perimeter-displacement opportunity, and it had added new monetisable layers on top of it. With FY2026 guidance already above **$3.3 billion** of revenue and ARR guidance above **$3.7 billion**, the company had room to argue that AI security, data protection and managed detection could expand wallet share inside an installed base that was already large and sticky [Q2 FY2026 results](https://ir.zscaler.com/news-releases/news-release-details/zscaler-announces-strong-second-quarter-fiscal-2026-results). The counterargument was equally clear. Broader product scope increased execution complexity, intensified competition and raised the burden on post-sale adoption. The outcome would turn less on whether zero trust remained relevant and more on whether Zscaler could remain the platform around which customers consolidated adjacent security spending.

---

## Product Glossary

**ZIA — Zscaler Internet Access.** Cloud-native secure web gateway and internet-access proxy. It replaced legacy on-premises firewalls, proxies and URL-filtering appliances and was delivered from Zscaler's global cloud fabric.

**ZPA — Zscaler Private Access.** Zero-trust network access for private applications. It replaced legacy VPN by connecting users to named applications rather than to the network itself.

**ZDX — Zscaler Digital Experience.** Digital experience monitoring for end-user visibility across devices, networks and applications.

**Zero Trust Exchange.** Zscaler's platform name for the combined policy-and-inspection fabric spanning ZIA, ZPA, ZDX, data protection, AI security and adjacent services.

**SASE — Secure Access Service Edge.** Gartner's term for the combination of networking and security services delivered from the cloud.

**SSE — Security Service Edge.** The security-only subset of SASE, including SWG, CASB, ZTNA and FWaaS.

**Risk360.** Zscaler's unified risk management and quantification layer, built in part on the Avalor acquisition.

| Cisco | Umbrella / Secure Connect / Catalyst SD-WAN stack | Public (CSCO, Nasdaq) |
